Begun
be-gun'
v. (past participle of begin; of a plague already spreading, of a conquest God announces as started, and of the good work God will perform)
From Old English beginnan, to begin. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 2:31 is chalal, to begin or make a start; the Greek at Philippians 1:6 is enarchomai, to begin in, set against epiteleo, to complete or bring to an end.

Biblical Definition

Three uses show the range. Of a judgment already in motion, and of an intercession made in haste: “Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from the LORD; the plague is begun” (Numbers 16:46). Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation and stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed — one of the clearest pictures of priestly mediation in the Pentateuch. Of a work God announces as already underway: “Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee: begin to possess, that thou mayest inherit his land” (Deuteronomy 2:31). God's beginning is the ground of Israel's beginning, and the order is never reversed. Moses uses the same word in prayer: “thou hast begun to shew thy servant thy greatness, and thy mighty hand” (Deuteronomy 3:24). Paul gives the word its greatest use: “Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) — the doctrine of perseverance stated as an inference from who started the work.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives begun as the participle of begin, and defines begin as to have an original or first existence, to take rise, to commence.

expand to see more

BEGUN, pp. of begin. Commenced; originated.

BEGIN, v.i. To have an original or first existence; to take rise; to commence.

As, the Christian era began in the fourth year of the four hundred and ninety-fourth Olympiad.

2. To do the first act; to enter upon something new.

BEGINNING, n. The first cause; origin. I am the beginning and the ending. Rev. 1.

Key Scripture

Philippians 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

Deuteronomy 2:31 — "And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee: begin to possess, that thou mayest inherit his land."

Deuteronomy 3:24 — "O Lord GOD, thou hast begun to shew thy servant thy greatness, and thy mighty hand: for what God is there in heaven or in earth, that can do according to thy works, and according to thy might?"

Numbers 16:46 — "And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from the LORD; the plague is begun."

Modern Corruption

Philippians 1:6 is applied to any personal ambition, when Paul's confidence rests entirely on the identity of the one who began the work.

expand to see more

The verse is printed on graduation cards and applied to careers, houses, and diets, with the sense that whatever a person has started God will help them finish. Paul's grammar will not carry it. The subject of both verbs is God: he which hath begun and will perform. The Philippians are the field, not the farmer, and Paul's confidence is not in their persistence but in the fact that the work was never theirs to start. This is the doctrine of perseverance of the saints in one sentence, and it is inseparable from effectual calling — the same God who began it is the one who guarantees the completion, and the guarantee is dated: until the day of Jesus Christ.

The Old Testament uses guard the doctrine from becoming passive. God says I have begun to give Sihon, and in the same breath says begin to possess. The divine beginning does not replace the human action; it commands and enables it, which is exactly Paul's work out your own salvation with fear and trembling: for it is God which worketh in you two chapters later in the same epistle. Numbers 16:46 shows the urgency the doctrine permits: the plague is begun, and Aaron runs. Confidence in God's finishing has never in Scripture produced a man standing still.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chalal, to begin — Deuteronomy 2:31, 3:24; Greek enarchomai, to begin in — Philippians 1:6; epiteleo, to complete — the paired verb.

expand to see more

Hebrew chalal — to begin, make a start; Deuteronomy 2:31, of God beginning to give Sihon.

Greek enarchomai — to begin in or among; Philippians 1:6 and Galatians 3:3.

Greek epiteleo — to complete, bring to an end; the answering verb, rendered perform.

Greek peitho — to be persuaded, confident; the participle behind “being confident.”

Hebrew magephah — a plague or stroke; Numbers 16:46, already begun when Aaron ran.

Usage

"“He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it” — both verbs have God as subject."

"“I have begun to give Sihon… begin to possess” — the divine start commands the human one."

"“The plague is begun” — and Aaron ran between the dead and the living."
